strings.path.title: Know the Neck
strings.path.goal: Find any natural note on any string, name the sharps and flats between them, see octaves, thirds and triads as shapes, play in G major and F major on the top three strings, and follow a chord progression in one position by name.
strings.path.assumes: You can fret and pick single notes and play quarter notes with a click at 70 BPM. You don't need to read music or know any scales. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; this is knowledge, and it sticks when you come back to it for a few minutes on many days.
strings.path.gradingLimits: The app checks that the notes you played were the written ones, after the take, and times them loosely. It cannot hear you say a note's name, and it cannot tell which string you played a pitch on: the same C on two strings sounds alike to it. So the saying and the place are yours to keep honest. The 'your turn' Exercises are not checked at all. None of this has been tried on a real guitar yet.

strings.step.low-strings.title: The low E and A strings
strings.step.low-strings.goal: Name and play every natural note on the low E and A strings up to the twelfth fret.
strings.step.low-strings.why: Barre chords, power chords and most scale shapes are named from the note under the first finger on one of these two strings. Know these two strings and you can name any chord you already play. The notes follow the alphabet from A to G, and these seven plain letters are called the natural notes. Each is two frets above the one before, which is called a whole step. The exceptions are B to C and E to F: they are next-door frets, a half step.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.0: The words this Path uses. The strings, from thickest to thinnest: low E, A, D, G, B and the top string. Fret 1 is the first space next to the nut, at the head end of the neck. Fingers are numbered from the index finger: first, second, third, and the little finger is the fourth.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.1: A click is the tick of the metronome. Each tick is a beat, four beats make a bar, and BPM is how many beats go by in a minute. A whole note lasts a whole bar, a half note two beats, a quarter note one beat. The pass tempo is the speed at which an Exercise counts as done.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.2: One play through an Exercise is a Take. Each Exercise has a ladder of tempos called rungs: between Takes, Slower and Faster move one rung along it, and the pass tempo is the rung at which the Exercise counts as done. Some Exercises change key or string from Take to Take.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.3: A key is the set of notes a piece of music uses. It is named after the note the music comes to rest on.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.4: Say each note's name out loud as you play it. Saying it is the practice; playing it is only the check.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.5: Walk up the string with the first finger alone. Two frets between most notes, one fret between B and C and between E and F.
strings.step.low-strings.howTo.6: The twelfth fret is the same note as the open string, an octave higher. The dots on the neck at 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are your landmarks.
strings.step.low-strings.payoff: You can put a finger on any fret of the two low strings and say what it is.

strings.step.octaves.title: Octave shapes
strings.step.octaves.goal: Find the same note an octave higher with one hand shape, from every string.
strings.step.octaves.why: An octave is the same note, higher. On the guitar it is a shape: two strings over and two frets up from the low E or A string, two strings over and three frets up from the D or G string. With it, the two strings you know name the other four.

strings.step.octaves.howTo.1: From the D or G string the shape is one fret wider, because of how the B string is tuned: first finger and little finger, three frets up.
strings.step.octaves.howTo.2: Say the note's name once for the pair. It is one note in two places.
strings.step.octaves.payoff: Every A on the neck, found in one take without hunting.

strings.step.chord-roots.title: The root of a chord you know
strings.step.chord-roots.goal: Find the root of E, A, D, G and C in the open chords you play, and the same root higher up the neck by the two octave shapes.
strings.step.chord-roots.why: A chord is named after one of its notes, the root. In the open chords E, A, D, G and C it is the lowest note you strum, on one of the three low strings, and you can name those now. If you do not play these chords yet, First Chords and Strumming teaches them, and this Step still works as single notes. The octave shapes then find the same root higher up, on the strings where the small chord shapes of later Steps sit. E minor, A minor and D minor have the same roots as E, A and D: the letter is the root, and the word after it says what kind of chord is built on it.
strings.step.chord-roots.howTo.0: E, A and D have their roots on open strings: the low E string, the A string and the D string. G is the low E string at fret 3. C is the A string at fret 3.
strings.step.chord-roots.howTo.1: From a root on the low E or A string, the octave is two strings over and two frets up. From the D or G string it is two strings over and three frets up.
strings.step.chord-roots.howTo.2: Say the chord's name as you play its root, and again for each octave. It is one note in several places.
strings.step.chord-roots.payoff: You can point to the root of every open chord here in two or three places, and walk the roots of three chords up the neck in time.

strings.step.upper-strings.title: The D, G and B strings
strings.step.upper-strings.goal: Name and play the natural notes on the D, G and B strings, and find one note on all six strings.
strings.step.upper-strings.why: The octave shape gets you to these strings; walking them by name makes them familiar. The B string is the odd one, tuned a fret lower than the pattern of the others, which is why every shape changes when it crosses onto it.

strings.step.upper-strings.howTo.1: Check any note with an octave shape back to the low E or A string if you are unsure.
strings.step.upper-strings.howTo.2: The top E string has the same notes as the low E string, two octaves up. You already know it.
strings.step.upper-strings.payoff: C on all six strings, one after another, with no hesitation.

strings.step.in-between.why: Every note in the Steps so far has been a plain letter, and every walk up a string has skipped frets. The skipped frets are notes too. Each one sits between two letters and takes its name from either neighbour: one fret above F is F sharp, and the same fret is one below G, so it is also G flat. Between E and F, and between B and C, there is no fret to skip, so there is no note in between. Chords and scales away from the natural notes need these: the scale of G major has an F sharp in it, and the scale of F major has a B flat.

strings.step.top-strings-keys.why: The walks up each string used the natural notes. Played in order from C, those seven are the C major scale. Music that uses them and comes to rest on C is in the key of C, and C is called its key note. Change the right one of the seven and you are in another key. G major is C major with F sharp in place of F. F major is C major with B flat in place of B. On each of the top three strings that is one fret moved, except that in F major the open B string itself drops out. Knowing which fret moves lets you name what you play in three keys instead of one.

strings.step.roots.title: Roots, fourths and fifths
strings.step.roots.goal: Find the roots of one, four and five, and of a minor four-chord song, on the low strings, by shape, and play them under a band.
strings.step.roots.why: Most songs move between a handful of chords. Count the notes of a key from its key note: in G that is G, A, B, C, D, E, F sharp. The chords on notes one, four and five, here G, C and D, are called the one chord, the four chord and the five chord, and a great many songs use only those three. Their roots sit in one small shape on the two low strings. Seeing that shape is how players follow a song they have never heard. Chords in a Key is the Path that explains these chords. Here you only find their roots.

strings.step.roots.howTo.1: The fifth of any note is also the top of its power chord: one string higher, two frets up.
strings.step.roots.howTo.2: Say the chord names as you change. In A the three are A, D and E.
strings.step.roots.payoff: You play the roots of a three-chord song in any key, and of a minor four-chord song, in time with a band.

strings.step.roots-other-keys.title: Roots in G and in D
strings.step.roots-other-keys.goal: Find the roots of one, four, five and of one, six, four, five in G and in D on the low E and A strings, by shape, and play them under a band.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.why: The shape from the last Step starts from a root on the low E string. A root on the A string turns it over: the five is at the same fret on the low E string, and the four is two frets below that. With both ways round, the roots of a song in G or in D are three or four places within a few frets of each other, and you can name each one as its chord arrives.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.howTo.0: From a root on the low E string, the four chord's root is at the same fret on the A string, and the five chord's root is two frets higher on the A string. In G: the low E string at fret 3, then the A string at 3 and at 5.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.howTo.1: From a root on the A string, the five chord's root is at the same fret on the low E string, and the four chord's root is two frets lower on the low E string. In D: the A string at fret 5, then the low E string at 5 and at 3.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.howTo.2: The six chord is the minor chord on the sixth note of the key: E minor in G, B minor in D. Its root is three frets below the one chord's root, on the same string: the open low E string in G, the A string at fret 2 in D.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.howTo.3: Say each root's name as its chord arrives. A minor chord's root is named like any other: E for E minor, B for B minor.
strings.step.roots-other-keys.payoff: You follow one, four, five and one, six, four, five in G and in D with a band, from a root on either of the two low strings.

strings.step.triads.title: Triads on the top strings
strings.step.triads.goal: Play a major and a minor triad in three places on the top three strings, and move between three chords with the nearest shapes.
strings.step.triads.why: A triad is the three notes a chord is made of: its root, the note a third above it, and the note a third above that, which is called the fifth because it is the fifth note of the scale counted from the root. The C triad is C, E and G. On the top three strings there are three shapes for each triad, depending on which note is on top, and together they cover the neck. This Step is a first look. Triads is the Path that builds them from the scale and moves them through the chords of a song.

strings.step.five-boxes.title: The five boxes, joined up
strings.step.five-boxes.goal: Play all five boxes of A minor pentatonic and move between them along two strings.
strings.step.five-boxes.why: The minor pentatonic scale has five notes. In A they are A, C, D, E and G. Up the neck those five notes make five overlapping shapes, called boxes. Box 1, at fret 5, is the one most players learn first, and Blues and Pentatonics teaches it and makes music with it in its first Step. If box 1 is new to you, learn it there first. This Step is a map of where all five are and how they join. The boxes are not five scales: they are one scale, and each box shares a wall with the next. Walking that wall on two strings is how the neck opens up.
strings.step.five-boxes.howTo.0: Box 1 of A minor pentatonic sits at fret 5, two notes on every string. The first finger plays fret 5 on all six strings. The other note is fret 8 with the little finger on the low E, B and top strings, and fret 7 with the third finger on the A, D and G strings.
strings.step.five-boxes.howTo.1: Each box starts on the next note of the scale on the low E string: A at fret 5, C at 8, D at 10, E at 12, G at 15 (or 3).
strings.step.five-boxes.howTo.2: The top notes of one box are the bottom notes of the next. Look for the frets they share.
strings.step.five-boxes.howTo.3: Find the A's in each box before you play it. They are your way home.
strings.step.five-boxes.payoff: One phrase that climbs three octaves, and a ladder up two strings through four of the boxes.

strings.step.arpeggios.title: Arpeggios up the neck
strings.step.arpeggios.goal: Play an A minor and a C major arpeggio from the low strings to the top, and four chords as arpeggios in one position.
strings.step.arpeggios.why: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time, and it is the surest way to sound like you know where you are in a song. Up the neck it links the triad shapes you know; in one position it shows that every chord of a song is already under your hand.

strings.step.the-changes.title: Following the changes
strings.step.the-changes.goal: Land on a note of each chord as a progression goes by, in one position, and know which note of the chord it is.
strings.step.the-changes.why: This is what the whole Path is for. A solo that follows the chords sounds like music; one that ignores them sounds like a scale. The trick is small: know where the root, third and fifth of each chord are under your hand, and be on one of them when the chord arrives.

strings.step.changes-in-g.title: Following the changes in G
strings.step.changes-in-g.goal: Land on a note of each chord over G, E minor, C and D in one position, say whether it is the root, the third or the fifth, and spell each chord as an arpeggio.
strings.step.changes-in-g.why: Following the changes over one progression can be a line you memorised. Over a second one, in another key, every landing has to be found again, and that is when it becomes something you can do. These four chords share notes: one note can be the root of one chord, the third of the next and the fifth of the one after. Hearing its job change while the finger stays put is the lesson here.

G: third finger, second finger, and the first finger flat across the B and top strings at fret 3. For E minor add the little finger on the B string at fret 5.

For C lift the second finger and lay the third finger flat so it takes the G string at fret 5 as well. The little finger and the first finger stay. It is the C shape at frets 3 to 5 from the Step on triads, with the D string added. There the second and third fingers held it; here the third and little fingers do, so that the little finger and the first finger can stay.

For D the hand moves down one fret: the third finger slides to fret 4 on the D string, the first finger lies flat across the G, B and top strings at fret 2, and the second finger takes the B string at fret 3. For G again the hand moves back up one fret.
